UAS University of Applied Sciences Flagship Initiative 4/19 1 The funding instrument “Flagship Initiative” The purpose of the flagship initiative is to stimulate innovation in areas relevant to a large part of the economy or society and to promote transdisciplinary project collaboration. The Ini- tiative strives for solutions to current or future challenges, which concern several actors and/or can only be solved through collaborative work. Innosuisse is therefore defining spe- cific but broad flagship topics in order to encourage applicants to address issues that are of particular interest for the future well-being of the country, and where new solutions and busi- ness models are required. This new funding instrument is complementary to the purely bot- tom-up oriented and well-established regular innovation projects. Systemic innovation, where value can only be derived if it is synergistically integrated with other complementary innovations, and transdisciplinarity, where actors from different disci- plines collaborate, are key components of this new funding instrument. The overall objective is to strengthen the competitiveness of the Swiss economy and/or con- tribute to the well-being of society by creating new value along the value chain by increasing efficiencies, reducing costs or re-solving social relevant challenges in the public interest. Under the Flagship Initiative, Innosuisse invites consortia to submit proposals for implement- ing flagship (Figure 1). Each flagship proposal consists of closely connected and interde- pendent subprojects (Figure 2). As a rule of thumb, a flagship should consist of three to eight sub-projects. Flagship proposals must be submitted by a consortium comprising multiple re- search and implementation partners from diverse disciplines (Figure 3). Figure 1: Flagship Initiative Structure Flagship Initiative 5/19 Figure 2: Example of a schematic representation showcasing the interrelation and interdependence of subprojects that collectively form a flagship. Figure 3: Structure of a consortium executing a flagship (example). Flagship Initiative 6/19 Flagships are characterized by a systemic, transdisciplinary perspective and a focus on prac- tical solutions. Priority is given to systemic innovation rather than the incremental improve- ment of existing systems (e.g., merely increasing efficiency or material properties). Instead, Flagships aim for long-term transformation, such as integrated mobility management or the circular economy. Crucially, it is not the result of a single subproject that drives change, but the synergy of inter- dependent subprojects working together. Therefore, strong transdisciplinary collaboration between academia and industry is essential. A proposed Flagship will only be considered if it demonstrates that the overall systemic result is greater than the sum of its individual parts. 1 E.g. Teece, 1986; Chesbrough and Teece, 2002; Kano, 2000; Gopalakrishnan and Bierly, 2001; Tay- lor and Levitt, 2004; Maula et al, 2006; Andersen and Drejer, 2008; van den Ende et al, 2008; Alin et al, 2013; Mlecnik, 2013; Takey and Carvalho, 2016) 2 https://www.basarab-nicolescu.ciret-transdisciplinarity.org/Docs_Notice/TJESNo_1_12_2010.pdf Definition of systemic innovation Systemic innovation is a type of innovation where value can only be derived if it is syner- gistically integrated with other complementary innovations, going beyond the boundaries of a single organization. Systemic innovation requires multiple innovations to be coordinated. Consequently, the different contributory innovations and organizations are organized to- gether into a whole system, where the overall success of the emergent innovation cannot be attributed to just one sub-innovation or participating organization. 1 Definition of transdisciplinarity Transdisciplinary is a way of thinking that rises above and beyond the methods of individ- ual disciplines, seeing multiple levels of meaning rather than simple dichotomies. Transdis- ciplinarity recognizes the existence of a complex and dynamic reality that transcends the boundaries of disciplines and requires a holistic and integrative approach. 2 Flagship Initiative 7/19 2 Call Announcement 2.1 Flagship topic of the call 2026 In an increasingly volatile security and geopolitical environment, physical and digital infra- structures, mobility systems and security-relevant applications are exposed to ever more complex threats. Technological dependencies on vulnerable or externally controlled systems can significantly restrict the ability of government, the economy and society to act. Resilient and secure key technologies that operate reliably under disrupted or hostile conditions are therefore essential to safeguard the long-term functioning of Swiss critical infrastructures and national security. The 2026 Flagship call is established as a joint and co-funded initiative between Innosuisse and armasuisse to address these challenges through the development of dual-use technolo- gies. This partnership aligns the strategic mandates of both organisations to strengthen Swit- zerland’s resilience and technological sovereignty. Simultaneously, the call is aligned with the 2025 armaments policy strategy of the Federal Council. The Flagship topic of the 2026 call is therefore: Resilient and Secure Technologies for Defence and Mobility To address this overarching objective effectively, the 2026 call concentrates on three com- plementary focus areas. They cover key technological enablers that are of strategic im- portance both for defence capabilities and for secure, highly available mobility. The Flagships are expected to develop systemic solutions that integrate one or several of these areas and thus make a measurable contribution to Switzerland’s technological sovereignty and resili- ence. The three focus areas of the call are: 1. Resilient positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) 2. Photonics for communication and sensor applications 3. Innovative technologies to counteract drones (C-UAV) The following sections describe these focus areas in more detail. Flagship Initiative 8/19 2.1.1 Resilient positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) Precise and reliable positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) systems already form the back- bone of modern society, the economy, national security and defence. Global navigation sat- ellite systems (GNSS) such as GPS and Galileo are essential for numerous critical infrastruc- tures. They not only determine precise location and movement for applications such as aviation and vehicle tracking but also provide highly accurate timing signals that synchronize critical infrastructures, including telecommunications networks, power grids, and financial transaction systems. However, GNSS signals are extremely weak and therefore particularly susceptible to radio frequency interference (jamming) and signal manipulation (spoofing). In recent years, the frequency of such interference, especially spoofing attacks, has increased dramatically. It is estimated that over one thousand flights are unintentionally affected by GNSS-spoofing every day. These disruptions are primarily caused by military electronic war- fare systems operated by state actors in conflict zones, used, for example, to defend against drones or to influence GPS-guided munitions. A GNSS failure is expected to have far-reaching and cascading consequences that go far beyond security-critical systems. Given the current vulnerability of GNSS-based PNT solu- tions, the use of multiple independent, complementary technologies to create a resilient over- all system is becoming increasingly important. Ensuring future-proof PNT capabilities re- quires both efforts to enhance the resilience and robustness of existing systems, and the development of alternative GNSS-independent technologies that do not rely on exposed in- frastructures. Such technologies offer significant potential in both civil domains, such as avia- tion, critical infrastructure, autonomous systems and emergency response, and in the field of defence, underlining their dual-use character and their overall economic and societal im- portance. Strengthening national PNT resilience across critical civil and security-related applications requires a trans- and interdisciplinary approach. The aim of this focus area is to foster sys- temic innovation that develops and demonstrates sovereign, complementary PNT solutions capable of improving GNSS resilience or operating independently of GNSS. This includes exploring and integrating a broad range of technologies, such as inertial sensors, quantum- based timing and navigation methods, precision clocks, innovative antennas, new anti-jam- ming algorithms and software-based solutions, while remaining open to additional technolo- gies and novel approaches. Also the integration of cyber resilience and anomaly detection is within scope to enhance the robustness and trustworthiness of PNT solutions. Flagship Initiative 9/19 2.1.2 Photonics for communication and sensor applications Photonics, the science of manipulating light, is becoming essential for modern defence tech- nologies. With evolving security threats, defence systems require advanced capabilities for rapid threat detection, secure communication, and reliable operation in complex environ- ments. Switzerland’s strong photonics research and innovative industry make it well-posi- tioned to develop cutting-edge photonics solutions that will strengthen national defence and technological sovereignty. The aim of the focus area is to develop next-generation photonic components and integrated systems specifically tailored for defence applications, while also enabling dual-use innova- tions with broad industrial impact. In scope are photonics technologies for sensor and com- munication applications (not limited to the examples below) such as: • Secure high-bandwidth optical communication technologies, incorporating quan- tum-safe encryption and anti-jamming features to protect sensitive defence infor- mation. • Quantum key distribution technologies and Quantum photonics techniques, to future-proof defence communication systems against emerging security threats. Ena- bling ultra-secure communication by using quantum mechanics principles to distribute encryption keys in a way that any interception attempt can be detected, making them highly relevant for protecting sensitive data. • Low probability of intercept optical communication channels to minimize detect- ability and resist electronic warfare and cyber-attacks. • High-power, tunable laser sources optimised for LIDAR applications, providing precise 3D mapping and target detection even in adverse weather or battlefield condi- tions. • Hyperspectral and thermal imaging sensors to enable detection of concealed threats through advanced spectral analysis and to enhance night vision capabilities. • Active imaging to image through camouflage, vegetation, smoke and fog. • Low-photon techniques and detection of optics for the affordable adoption of high-performance photon counting technologies in active and passive imaging includ- ing advanced SPAD (Single-Photon Avalanche Diode) technologies. Retroreflection detection is a powerful means of locating adversary sighting systems. Low-photon techniques reduce the probability that retroreflection systems themselves are de- tected. • Low-power neuromorphic imaging and computing optimized for military appli- cations, where digital readout technology of neuromorphic sensors promises to re- duce electrooptical/infrared (EO/IR) system costs and power consumption while deliv- ering greater performance compared to conventional sensor designs. Neuromorphic inspired pre-processing framework combining optical-domain and electronic compu- ting to accelerate onboard image processing. The call encourages interdisciplinary approaches that leverage Switzerland’s strengths in photonics, quantum technologies, space technologies, artificial intelligence, and systems in- tegration to deliver innovative photonics solutions with relevance for both defence and civilian applications. Flagship Initiative 10/19 2.1.3 Innovative technologies to counteract drones (C-UAV) Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) pose a major challenge to the security of society, the economy and critical infrastructure. The rapidly increasing availability and advancing technol- ogy of drones are creating new opportunities for both civilian and government actors, but at the same time they pose substantial risks through hostile use. Counter-UAV (C-UAV) sys- tems are therefore crucial to effectively mitigate threats related to hybrid conflicts and war- fare, including espionage, sabotage, and attacks on critical infrastructure. The strategic im- portance of C-UAV technologies will continue to grow in the coming years and is vital not only on the battlefield but also for protecting airports, urban areas and other critical infrastruc- tures. Current C-UAV systems face various challenges. Limited detection accuracy for discriminat- ing drones from other flying objects such as birds and the limited detection range make it dif- ficult to identify drones. Additionally, the speed and manoeuvrability of drones make it difficult to detect drones quickly and the limited response time makes it even more challenging to take effective countermeasures in time. The ongoing improvements in drone technology are resulting in an evolving threat landscape. Some drones contain signature-reducing technolo- gies or are equipped with jamming/spoofing protection technologies, making current mitiga- tion strategies less effective. Furthermore, fibre-optic cable drones, capable of operating over distances up to 50 km, have been used in Ukraine, and coordinated drone swarms are ex- pected to be the next major threat. In addition to the technical and tactical challenges, there is also the challenge posed by the asymmetry of costs, which currently favours the attackers. The measures required to defend against attacks can far exceed the cost of the attacking drone itself. This leads to the consumption of expensive ammunition that is actually designed for combating high-value assets. In addition, collateral damage risks arising from the counter- measures must be reduced. C-UAV systems consist of three key elements: • Detection, identification and tracking, through technologies such as advanced sensor and radar technologies, radio frequency spectrum monitoring, electro-optical and infrared imaging and acoustic detection arrays. • Resilient command & control architecture, including multi-modal sensor fusion and integration platforms and software-based solutions. • Active counter-drone measures, such as directed energy weapons, electronic war- fare systems, kinetic interceptor systems and drone interceptors. The development of effective and deployable C-UAV systems requires a transdisciplinary ap- proach. Only by doing so can solutions be created that meet the high requirements for safety and efficiency and consider the legal and ethical challenges. The Flagship Initiative aims to promote systemic innovation that contributes significantly to strengthening national resilience and protection of the population and infrastructure from hostile drone threats. Flagship Initiative 11/19 2.2 Eligible structure and call specifications Partners The invitation to tender is addressed to consortia comprising both research 3 and implementa- tion 4 partners. The consortium consists of at least three research partners, of which at least one is a university of applied sciences, and at least two implementation partners. Only research institutions that are recognised as eligible research partners by Innosuisse may participate as research partners in a Flagship. In order to be eligible as a non-commercial research centre outside of the higher education sector and to submit an application for contributions to innovation projects, the research cen- tre must meet the requirements of Article 5 RIPA and Article 10 of the Innosuisse’s imple- menting provisions for innovation projects. These requirements are outlined in the following information sheet: Information on the requirements and criteria for non-commercial research centres outside the higher education sector Important: All documents required for non-commercial research centres outside the higher education sector must already be submitted at the pre-proposal stage. The final eligibility de- cision for the same organisation is taken during the proposal phase. If the result of the eligi- bility review is negative, the funding application for a project is not materially assessed and a non-consideration decision is taken. The Flagship should only include implementation partners who make a substantial contribu- tion to the project’s execution and implementation. In addition, for the purposes of this call, the Federal Office for Defence Procurement (armasuisse) will not be available as an imple- mentation partner. While Innosuisse does not prescribe the internal organization of the consortium, a Higher Ed- ucation Institution (HEI) or a non-commercial research institution outside the university sec- tor 5 must act as the Host Institution taking over the role of the funding management body 6 . The Host Institution represents the project partners vis-à-vis Innosuisse during the applica- tion process and throughout the Flagship's duration. Furthermore, it must appoint a repre- sentative to serve as the primary point of contact for Innosuisse. During the implementation phase, the consortium composition may change (new partners joining or existing ones withdrawing), provided that the original objectives remain unaffected and contractual conditions are upheld. Any such changes require prior written approval from Innosuisse and, where necessary, a corresponding contract amendment. 3 Definition of research partner according to Art. 7 Innosuisse funding ordinance (as of 1.1.2023) 4 Implementation partners are private or public institutions or companies that ensure implementation, Art. 19 para. 1 RIPA (as of 1.1.2023) 5 Art. 5 RIPA 6 Art. 13 Innosuisse Funding Ordinance as well as Art. 13 of the Implementing Provisions for Innova- tion Projects. Flagship Initiative 12/19 Dual-Use requirement Flagship proposals submitted in the framework of the Call 2026 and their targeted innova- tions must be designed to provide a clear dual-use perspective, i.e. they must be relevant for both civil and defence-related applications. Projects that pursue a purely defence or a purely civil single-use objective are not eligible for funding under this call. This dual-use character will be explicitly queried in the application forms and must be substantiated by the consortium in the (pre-)proposal. Ethics and research security Ethics and knowledge-/research security play an important role in this call. Innosuisse promotes innovations that meet ethical standards, which translates in behaviour and intentions not harming the dignity of humans and animals, life, health, freedom, property, the environment, or peaceful coexistence. Knowledge & research security refers to the prevention of the unwanted transfer of sensitive information, know-how, and technology, the mitigation of foreign interference in higher edu- cation and research, and the reduction of dependencies that could endanger national secu- rity and competitiveness. The aim of knowledge & research security is to protect core scien- tific values, innovative ideas, ensure that international cooperation remains ethical and safe, and safeguard national interests and values. Project partners must duly consider these aspects in the design and conduct of their project as well as in their risk analysis (ethics and knowledge & research security by design). Spe- cific questions on ethics and research security will be integrated into the application forms and the evaluation process. Innosuisse may carry out background checks if needed. Duration There are no strict conditions regarding the duration of a Flagship. However, it is anticipated that a Flagship will exceed the duration of a standard Innosuisse innovation project due to its systemic approach and transdisciplinary nature. Budget The regulations governing Innosuisse innovation projects apply (see Chapter 3). Flagship Initiative 13/19 2.3 Dates and deadlines in 2026 and 2027 Date What Who 1 July 2026 Launch of the call 2026 Innosuisse 13 August 2026 Webinar Innosuisse 20 August 2026 Deadline for written questions Applicants 1 September 2026 Publication of Q&A (FAQ) on Innosuisse website Innosuisse 27 October 2026 (12 o’clock / noon) Submission deadline: Pre-proposal Applicants February 2027 Dispatch of recommendation letters Innosuisse 4 May 2027 (12 o’clock / noon) Submission deadline: Proposal Applicants July 2027 Notification of decision Innosuisse August 2027 Provision of Funding Agreements Innosuisse Q4 2027 / Q1 2028 Start of funded flagships Applicants 3 Finances 3.1 General principles Innosuisse funding covers the personnel costs of research partners, including overhead and employer contributions, as well as material costs. Additionally, a dedicated portion of the budget may be allocated to management and coordination of the overall flagship initiative. 3.2 Eligible costs Personnel costs Personnel costs are eligible according to the Innosuisse funding ordinance (Art. 9, 10 and 12) and the implementing provisions for innovation projects (Art. 15 to 17). Innosuisse fund- ing covers the effective wage costs of the research partner incl. overhead and employer con- tribution. The personnel costs are calculated either using evidence of the gross salaries paid or the ap- plicable notional hourly rates according to article 16 and 17 of the implementing provisions for innovation projects. Material costs Material costs are eligible according to the Innosuisse funding ordinance (Art. 9) and the im- plementing provisions for funding innovation projects (Art. 18). Only costs that are actually incurred and are absolutely necessary for the proper execution of the flagship are taken into account. All the planned material costs need to be included in the proposal. Coordination costs Certain coordination costs can be covered within this category which necessarily arise due to a coordination effort between the project partners, which is particularly high compared to or- dinary national innovation projects, and which are not covered by personnel or material costs according to the implementing provisions for funding innovation projects (Art. 19). Flagship Initiative 14/19 3.3 Financing conditions Innosuisse covers a certain amount of the direct costs of a flagship. The funds provided by Innosuisse flow exclusively and directly to the research partners and never to the implemen- tation partners. The legal basis allows an Innosuisse contribution of 40 to 60%. The imple- mentation partners contribute to the total costs of the flagship to the extent of 40 to 60% of the eligible direct overall project costs. This contribution comprises own work and services as well as a financial contribution to the research partners. The financial contribution amount to at least 5% of the overall project costs according to the Innosuisse funding ordinance (Art. 11). 4 Submission and Evaluation of an application The application process is competitive and will be a 2-step procedure (Figure 4 and 5): pre- proposal and proposal. Submission of a pre-proposal is a mandatory prerequisite for submit- ting a full proposal. The proposal must be submitted in English, German, French or Italian. Applications must be submitted via Innolink, in accordance with the information on the Inno- suisse homepage. Important information on roles and responsibilities of Innosuisse and armasuisse: In the context of this joint call, armasuisse has contributed to the definition of the topics and co-finances the call. The entire call, submission and evaluation process, however, is carried out according to the established procedures of Innosuisse. All evaluation steps are con- ducted under the responsibility of Innosuisse, and the funding decisions are taken exclusively by Innosuisse. armasuisse is not involved in the evaluation of applications or in the funding decisions and, for the purposes of this call, will not be available as an implementation part- ner.
